description: We are a team of passionate and innovative students interested in space science, technology, artificial intelligence, and problem-solving. Our goal is to collaborate, learn new skills, and develop creative solutions to real-world challenges using NASA's open data. We welcome enthusiastic teammates with skills in programming, AI/ML, data analysis, web development, research, design, and presentation who are ready to learn, share ideas, and innovate together.

details:
What it does and how it works
TerraCycle AI helps farmers in Karnataka, India compare crop rotations before they plant. It uses 20 years (2005-2024) of NASA POWER climate data, local soil classes, crop traits and the farmer’s own priorities. It compares three strategies (existing, water-resilient and soil-restoring) and scores each out of 100 on water use, soil health, climate resilience, income and rotation fit. Rotation fit looks at the sequence, not just single crops. It checks for repeated crop families, nitrogen-fixing legumes before cereals, root-depth variety, bare periods without ground cover, and pest and disease conflicts.

Farmers set priority sliders for what matters most to them. The weights always total 100, so the same data gives a different ranking for a farmer focused on water than for one focused on income.

Climate shock simulator
Users can test every rotation under 20% less rain, 40% less rain, 2 °C of warming, or both combined. Rankings update live. Results are always labelled “simulation, not a forecast.”

Honest and explainable
Every score shows its reasoning, evidence, risks and uncertainties. Each data point carries a badge: observed, estimated, assumed, simulated or needs expert. Only the climate data is observed. Soil and crop data are assumed and flagged for validation, and we state that NDVI vegetation data and measured soil carbon are not yet used.

Benefits and intended impact
Farmers can see risk before a season is lost, protect soil, save water and plan for a changing climate. The tool supports the farmer’s judgment and never replaces it.

Tools and technology
A browser-based tool built with vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks or external dependencies), with NASA POWER data prepared as JSON files for climate, soil, crops and rotation rules. The engine has separate modules for climate scenarios, rotation analysis and scoring, each with built-in self-tests.

What makes it creative
Instead of a black-box “AI” prediction, it uses a transparent scoring model, so farmers can see why a rotation ranks where it does. Combining sequence-aware rotation analysis with a live climate simulator and honest data labelling sets it apart.

Factors we considered
Rainfall seasonality, drought years, heat, soil water holding and erosion risk, crop water needs and drought tolerance, nitrogen effects, pests, market value, and the farmer’s priorities. Next steps are NASA SMAP, GPM and MODIS data, farmer soil-test input, and validation with local agronomists and KVK experts.
